hints: Focus on the two things that control the speed here, how easily the carbon-halogen bond breaks and how good the attacking nucleophile is.
Compare the halogens first, the $\text{C-Br}$ bond is longer and weaker than the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond, so bromoalkanes react faster.
Now compare the reagents, the negatively charged hydroxide ion is a much stronger nucleophile than neutral water, so pair the best halogen with the best nucleophile.
walkthrough:
**Understand the reaction type**

Hydrolysis of a primary halogenoalkane is nucleophilic substitution. The nucleophile attacks the $\delta+$ carbon and the halide leaves.

$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{X} + \text{OH}^- / \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{X}^-$$

**Compare the C-X bond strength**

Breaking the $\text{C-X}$ bond is key to the rate. Bond strength increases up Group 17.

$$\text{C-Br weaker than C-Cl, so it breaks more easily}$$ 
That means $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ hydrolyses faster than $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ under the same conditions.

**Compare the strength of the nucleophile**

Neutral $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is a weak nucleophile. Aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ provides $\text{OH}^-$, which is negatively charged and a much stronger nucleophile.

$$\text{nucleophile strength: OH}^- > \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ 
A stronger nucleophile attacks faster, so reaction with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ is much faster than with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

**Combine both effects**

Fastest halogen is Br. Fastest reagent is $\text{NaOH(aq)}$. Put them together and you get the most rapid hydrolysis at the same temperature.

options.A: This has the more reactive bromoalkane, which is good, but water is a weak neutral nucleophile. It will be faster than the chloroalkane with water, but slower than reaction with hydroxide.
options.B: This combines both rate-enhancing factors. The weak $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks easily and the strong $\text{OH}^-$ nucleophile attacks rapidly, giving the fastest nucleophilic substitution.
options.C: This is the slowest combination. It has the stronger $\text{C-Cl}$ bond which is harder to break, plus the weak $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ nucleophile, so hydrolysis is very slow.
options.D: This benefits from the strong $\text{OH}^-$ nucleophile, so it is faster than with water, but the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is stronger than $\text{C-Br}$. It loses to the bromoalkane with the same reagent.
